claims.text: The unchanged (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a large caloric response under applied magnetic-field and pressure-field stimuli.
The unchanged alloy has poor mechanical integrity and tends to crack under mechanical stress.
Controlled mild oxidation during processing can generate a finely dispersed nanoscale Mn- or Fe-based oxide phase in the alloy.
The oxide nanoparticles will be distributed uniformly at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
An in-situ-generated secondary-particle dispersion can reinforce a high-entropy-alloy microstructure and increase its strength.
The oxide nanoparticles will inhibit crack initiation and propagation through particle-induced bridging and pinning.
A low oxide volume fraction will avoid formation of a continuous secondary phase that could hinder the caloric transformation.
The oxide phase will be chemically compatible with the matrix and will not disrupt the crystallographic phase transition responsible for the caloric effect.
Epoxy and low-melting-metal reinforcements can adversely affect overall performance because of their different thermal conductivities or mechanical properties.
The unmodified alloy has compressive strength below 100 MPa or comparably low integrity.
Oxide-dispersion reinforcement will raise the alloy's compressive strength into the 150–220 MPa range or higher.
The modified alloy will retain approximately the same caloric entropy change as the unmodified alloy.
Both the magnetic-field-driven and pressure-driven caloric responses will remain nearly unchanged in magnitude and transition sharpness.
The proposed benefit requires an oxide fraction below 10 vol% and particle sizes on the order of tens of nanometers.
Over-oxidation that produces abundant or large oxide phases will invalidate the proposed mechanical and caloric enhancement.
The enhancement will remain applicable under moderate applied fields and pressures, near-transition temperatures, and compression or bending loads at room-to-moderate temperatures.
